newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Students march on Milosevic's Belgrade home.
newsitem.headline: Students march on Milosevic's Belgrade home.

text.p: Serbian students on Wednesday marched towards President Slobodan Milosevic's home to pressure him to allow opposition election victories they say were stolen by ruling socialists.
Some 30,000 students marched for the second time in a week on Dedinje, the exclusive residential area in Belgrade that houses Milosevic and members of his privileged ruling elite.

Police in riot gear politely but resolutely turned them back on approaches to the district, continuing the measured policy that has characterised their behaviour since vast opposition protests against Milosevic's Socialists began a month ago.
The students carried a large cardboard pyramid inscribed with the words "Forbidden City, No Trespassing." They planned to leave it where police stopped them.

The students and opposition are protesting against alleged election fraud which cheated the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition of victory in 15 of the biggest Serbian cities, including Belgrade, in November 17 local elections.

The daily demonstrations which drew up to 250,000 people last weekend and spread to more than 30 cities, have forced the authorities to concede opposition victory in the southern town of Smederevska Palanka and the industrial centre of Nis.
But the biggest prize -- control of the capital Belgrade -- has yet to be won.
Washington has led Western attacks on effective one-party rule in Serbia, demanding that Milosevic accept defeat in Belgrade and other towns.

Popular pressure and Western displeasure seemed to be behind Milosevic's pledge on Tuesday to students, who trekked on foot for 230 km (145 miles) to meet him, that he would investigate opposition protests against vote rigging.

"Neither you nor I count votes, but I shall ask the government to instruct the justice ministry to very carefully study all the facts contained in the documents which you have given me," Milosevic told the students.

At the meeting, later broadcast on state-run television which has carried scant footage of the protests, he said: "Mistakes are always possible...I assure you that this state will not protect anyone who has broken the law, be they citizens or officials."

To soothe his hardliners who are increasingly calling for action, Milosevic added: "We must also make it very clear that regardless of any visits your leaders make to embassies or foreign capitals, a foreign hand will never govern Serbia."
Milosevic met leading officials of his Socialist party on Tuesday night to discuss strategy as Zajedno vowed to flood the streets of Serbia with people again on Wednesday.
In a sign that Milosevic might give way in Belgrade Zajedno said the Serbian supreme court had upheld its victory in the Savski Venac municipality.
But Milosevic might wait for the arrival of a team from the Organisation for Cooperation and Security in Europe which he invited to verify the results.
The OSCE team, headed by former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, should arrive before Christmas.
